opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core reason is humility about what we don't know. When you design a cipher like AES, you're making a bet that will have to hold for decades, against attackers you can't predict, using techniques that haven't been invented yet. History is full of schemes that looked fine at first and then fell apart. MD5 and SHA-1 are good examples. Attacks only get better; they never get worse. So you deliberately build in far more strength than today's best attack requires.

With AES-256, the best known attacks barely dent the full cipher. You're still astronomically far from anything practical. You could lose a lot of rounds' worth of security to some clever new cryptanalysis and still be completely safe. That margin is what lets people sleep at night.

And the cost of that margin is tiny. A few extra rounds, a slightly longer key, a little more computation. Compare that with the cost of being wrong, where every piece of data ever encrypted under the scheme is exposed. When the downside is catastrophic and irreversible, and the insurance is cheap, you buy a lot of insurance.

The reason I find this interesting is the contrast with machine learning, and especially adversarial robustness and AI safety. In ML we often do the opposite. Someone proposes a defense, it survives the attacks the authors thought to try, and we call it robust. Then a few months later someone, sometimes me, breaks it with a slightly better attack. We have essentially zero security margin. We're shipping systems at the very edge of what we've managed to evaluate, and assuming attackers won't be any smarter than we are.

So when I think about how we should handle powerful AI systems, I'd love to see more of the cryptographer's mindset. Assume the adversary is smarter than you. Assume your evaluations are incomplete. Leave a lot of room between "this is what we've tested" and "this is what we're relying on." Cryptographers learned that lesson the hard way, and I'd rather we didn't have to learn it the hard way too.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is: cryptographers are the one community in computer security that has really internalized that attacks only get better. They never get worse. When you design a cipher, you're not designing it against the attacks that exist today; you're designing it against every attack anyone will come up with over the next thirty or forty years, including attacks from techniques that haven't been invented yet.

AES-256 is a nice example. If you look at the best known attacks on full-round AES, they're nowhere close to practical. We're talking about shaving off a couple of bits from the key space, or attacks that only work against reduced-round variants. So you might say, well, 128 bits was plenty, why go to 256? And the answer is that the extra margin costs almost nothing. It's a few more rounds, a little more computation, and in exchange you buy insurance against the thing you didn't anticipate. Quantum computers are the obvious case: Grover's algorithm roughly halves your effective key length, and AES-256 just absorbs that. Nobody in 2001 was building that in because they had a quantum computer sitting around. They built it in because they knew they didn't know what was coming.

And there's a broader principle here that I think about a lot coming from the machine learning side. Cryptographers have this culture where the attacker is assumed to be smarter than you, better resourced than you, and patient. The default posture is humility. If the best attack you can find is a factor of two better than brute force, you don't say "great, we're still safe." You say "that's a crack, and cracks widen." Several ciphers have been retired not because they were practically broken, but because the margin had eroded enough that people stopped trusting them.

Contrast that with how a lot of the rest of the field works, and especially with how we've approached adversarial robustness in ML. The pattern there, over and over, has been that someone proposes a defense, evaluates it against the attacks they happen to know about, declares victory, and then a few months later somebody adapts the attack slightly and the defense falls over completely. There's no margin. It's broken by a factor of a thousand, not a factor of two. If we'd had the cryptographer's mindset of "assume the attacker adapts, assume they're cleverer than my evaluation," a lot of that work would have been more careful from the start.

So I think the large margins aren't really about AES specifically. They're an expression of an epistemic position: you're uncertain about the future capabilities of your adversary, and the asymmetry is that being too conservative costs you a little efficiency, while being too optimistic costs you everything. When the downside is that lopsided, you should overbuild. The cryptographers just figured that out earlier than the rest of us.

astra-6.text:
Because attacks get better. When we design a cryptographic system, we’re not just trying to defend against the best attack we know today. We’re trying to defend against attacks that someone might discover twenty or thirty years from now. And predicting those discoveries is extremely hard.

So you want room to be wrong. If someone finds a way to make an attack a trillion times faster, that sounds catastrophic—and it would be if your system were only barely secure. But with a sufficiently large security margin, that improvement can still leave the attack completely infeasible.

And the cost of that margin is relatively small. Using AES-256 doesn’t make encryption astronomically more expensive than using a smaller key. You pay a modest cost now to protect against a lot of uncertainty later. That’s a very good trade.

sol-6.1.text:
Because attacks get better. As a cryptographer, you don’t want to design something that’s just barely secure against the best attack you know today. You want it to remain secure even after somebody comes up with a much cleverer attack ten or twenty years from now.

AES-256 gives you an enormous amount of room. If somebody finds an attack that reduces the work from roughly two to the 256 to two to the 128, that’s a spectacular cryptanalytic advance, but it still doesn’t make the system practically breakable. That’s exactly what you want a security margin to do: absorb surprises.

And the cost of that extra margin is relatively small compared with the cost of discovering, after everyone has deployed your system, that you were too optimistic.
